title: Do education programmes for children and young people with disabilities in low- and middle-income countries work?

blocks.html: The question is: “In low- and middle-income countries, do programmes meant to improve education for children and young people with disabilities work, and which kinds work best?”

sentences: A 2025 Campbell systematic review concludes that a range of individual-level interventions work to improve educational outcomes among people with disabilities in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), but that there is little research on systemic or school-level change [1].

The interventions that work are mostly targeted at people with disabilities themselves, and the review's authors say more systemic approaches are needed to improve rates of access to, and likelihood of successful engagement in, education [1].

The clearest effects reported are for interventions building 'Skills for learning', with significant, large effects on literacy, cognitive skills, handwriting and numeracy, though these are based on a low number of studies [1].
People with disabilities often fall behind in education compared to their peers without disabilities, in enrolment, retention and completion [1].
Evidence suggests that the gap in educational attainment between people with and without disabilities is greatest in LMICs [1].
These inequalities contribute to people with disabilities being less likely to gain employment, or to earn as much if they are employed [1].
According to the source, "All but one study received an overall rating of low confidence in study findings." [1]

According to the source, a twin-track approach is needed, which both addresses the specific needs of children with disabilities but also ensures that they are included in mainstream activities (e.g., through improving the skills of teachers and accessibility of the classroom) [1].

According to the source, currently most interventions included in this systematic review targeted individual children with disabilities in an attempt to improve their functioning, skills, and competencies, but did not focus on mainstreaming these children into the school by system-level or school-level changes [1].
The source states: "Consequently, a focus on evaluation of interventions which target not just the individual with a disability but also their broader environment, are needed." [1]

According to the source, the evidence and gap map (EGM) summarized here "provides a starting point for researchers, decision makers and programme managers to access the available research evidence on the effectiveness of interventions for people with disabilities in LMICs in order to guide policy and programme activity, and encourage a more strategic, policy‐oriented approach to setting the future research agenda." [2]

According to the source, "This report illustrates the critical value of evaluating and publishing evidence from disability inclusive TPD interventions in LMICs, including any that are ongoing, or are components of highly resource intensive large‐scale education sector programs." [3]

The source is titled "Teacher professional development for disability inclusion in low‐ and middle‐income Asia‐Pacific countries: An evidence and gap map," and the text provided contains no certainty or confidence wording, so no findings can be stated with a degree of certainty [3].
Among the 18 studies included in the review's analysis of intervention effects on 'Skills for learning', 12 interventions had a significant effect [1].
Looking across outcomes, the effects on literacy, cognitive skills, handwriting and numeracy are significant, and all of these effects are large but rest on a low number of studies [1].
Included studies concerned with 'Conditions for inclusion of people with disabilities in education' showed a moderately significant effect [1].
One study concerned with teacher knowledge showed a significant effect size [1].

The second most common category of intervention was 'Accessible learning environments', for instance programmes aiming to improve social skills or to reduce victimisation of children with disabilities in schools [1].

An evidence and gap map found 50 studies on teacher training for the inclusion of students with disabilities in low- and middle-income Asia-Pacific countries, but only 16 of 41 countries reported evidence on in-service teacher professional development for disability inclusion [3].
That map found no studies reporting on how teachers could support positive student behaviour [3].
In one qualitative study from Vietnam, teachers reported that training seminars and workshops improved the general quality of teaching in their schools [3].
An earlier evidence and gap map on disability interventions reported only a single study on in-service teacher professional development, from Kenya [3].

An evidence and gap map of disability interventions in LMICs found that studies focus on fixing individuals, for instance improving social or learning skills, and that fewer studies focus on improving infrastructure or institutions [2].

That is, the interventions mostly try to change characteristics of the person with a disability rather than address structures such as the readiness of schools to include people with learning disabilities [2].
The map's authors call the absence of evidence on what works to promote disability inclusion a very striking gap [2].
Most studies come from upper-middle income countries, with limited evidence from low-income countries [2].
More studies are needed on all types of impairment, including visual and hearing impairments [2].
The studies concerned with speech and school behaviour show no significant effect of intervention [1].
Across the studies reviewed, heterogeneity is high, and the risk of publication bias varies but was frequently high [1].
All but one of the included studies were rated low confidence in their findings, so the evidence on whether these programmes work is weak [1].
The review found that low confidence across studies was largely due to the use of low-rigour study designs, and did not always reflect multiple points of weakness within a given study [1].

The source says a twin-track approach is needed, one that addresses the specific needs of children with disabilities while also including them in mainstream activities, for example by improving teachers' skills and classroom accessibility [1].

Most interventions in the systematic review targeted individual children with disabilities to improve their functioning, skills and competencies, rather than mainstreaming them through system-level or school-level changes [1].
The sources say that evaluation should focus on interventions that target not just the individual with a disability but also their broader environment [1].
Only three studies reported interventions aimed at supporting mental health among students with a disability, so evidence on this type of programme is sparse [3].

It holds up that a range of interventions aimed at individual learners with disabilities in LMICs work to improve educational outcomes, with the strongest reported effects on literacy, cognitive skills, handwriting and numeracy [1].
Those large effects come from a low number of studies, so the size of the benefit is less certain than its direction [1].
Evidence on interventions that change conditions for inclusion, including teacher knowledge, is thinner, though it showed a moderately significant effect [1].
Which kinds work best cannot be firmly settled, because research on systemic or school-level change is scarce rather than shown to be ineffective [1, 2].
The effects reported above are broken down by outcome and intervention category, not by type of disability, so they do not show which interventions work best for which disabilities.
Evidence from low-income countries is limited, so findings drawn mostly from upper-middle income countries may not carry over directly [2].

blocks.html:
We hold the full text of Effectiveness of interventions for improving educational outcomes for people wit [1].

We searched the full text of Effectiveness of interventions for improving educational outcomes for people wit [1] and checked the passages relevant to each sentence; we did not read it in full.

We found Evidence and gap map of studies assessing the effectiveness of interventions for people with disabilities in low-and middle-income countries but it has a published correction we could not hold, so nothing on this page draws on it.

We found Teacher professional development for disability inclusion in low- and middle-income Asia-Pacific countries: An evidence and gap map but it has a published correction we could not read, so nothing on this page draws on it.

We searched the full text of PROTOCOL: Effectiveness of interventions for improving educational outcomes for [4] and checked the passages relevant to each sentence; we did not read it in full.

We searched: web search: systematic review inclusive education children disabilities low middle income countries; web search: disability inclusive education interventions LMIC effectiveness review; web search: evidence gap map disability education interventions LMIC White Kuper Campbell; web search: UNESCO guidelines inclusive education disability developing countries policy; web search: Wapling systematic review disability education strategies LMIC 2016; web search: UNICEF "effectiveness of inclusive interventions" children disabilities 2022 education; web search: teacher professional development disability inclusion Asia-Pacific LMIC evidence gap map Campbell 2023; registry: Europe PMC.

We did not search: trial registries; Crossref; MEDLINE, Embase and CENTRAL directly; national guidelines.
